en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Chapter on the Painted Hall, 46.
The Training Rule on the Gift of Food:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was personally giving hard and soft food to actors, dancers, acrobats, jesters, and tumblers, saying:
"Praise me in my assembly.
And the actors, dancers, acrobats, jesters, and tumblers praised the bhikkhunī Thullanandā in her assembly.
“The noble lady Thullanandā is learned, an eloquent speaker, confident, and capable of delivering a discourse on the Dhamma;
give it to the noble lady, let the noble lady do so!
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How indeed can the noble lady Thullanandā give hard food and soft food with her own hand to a householder?
… [as before] … “Is it true, monks, that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā gives hard food and soft food with her own hand to a householder?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her:
“… How indeed, monks, can the nun Thullanandā give hard food and soft food with her own hand to a householder?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of the faithful…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule as follows:
“Whichever nun should, with her own hand, give fresh or cooked food to a householder, or to a male wanderer, or to a female wanderer, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
“Whichever nun” means:
Whichever [nun] of such a kind... "a nun" ...pe...
this is the nun intended in this context.
A householder is anyone who dwells in a house.
A wanderer is...
Except for a bhikkhu and a sāmaṇera, anyone who has entered the state of a wanderer (paribbājaka).
A female wanderer (paribbājikā) is anyone who has entered the state of a female wanderer, except for a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, and a sāmaṇerī.
"Solid food" means the five kinds of cooked food;
with the exception of water and tooth-sticks, the remainder is called "solid food."
"Eatable" means the five kinds of staple foods: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat.
"Should give" means...
If she gives it with her own body, or with something connected to her body, or with something that has been relinquished, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she gives water or a tooth-stick, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense—
He causes [another] to give but does not give himself;
he gives after having set it aside;
he gives an external ointment.
“[If she is] insane,” “if she is a first-offender.
The sixth training rule is finished.
